title: Adulting 101
tagline: Rent, insurance, doctors, cars, cooking and paperwork, handled.
description: The practical skills nobody hands you a manual for: renting your first place, choosing insurance, getting the right medical care, and keeping a car running. You will also learn the home fixes that save a service call, how to eat well on a budget without getting sick, and how to keep your important documents safe.

units.title: Your First Place
units.description: Find an apartment you can afford, read the lease, protect your deposit and handle basic fixes.

levels.title: Finding and Leasing an Apartment
levels.summary: How much rent you can afford, what landlords check, and lease fine print.

steps.title: How much rent can you afford?
steps.body:
A common guideline: keep rent at or below about **30% of your gross monthly income** (your pay before taxes).

Example: you earn $2,500 a month before taxes. 30% of that is $750, so look for rent around $750 or less.

> Rent is not your only housing cost. Utilities (power, water, internet), renter's insurance, parking and getting to work add up too.
steps.tip: Before you tour apartments, ask each landlord which utilities are included and what the average monthly bill is. Add that to the rent before you compare places.

steps.prompt: You earn $3,000 a month before taxes. Using the 30% guideline, what is the most you should spend on rent each month?
steps.explain:
$3,000 x 0.30 = **$900**.

Quick way: 10% of $3,000 is $300, and 30% is three times that: $900.

Higher rent is possible, but it squeezes savings and everything else.
steps.hint: 30% is the same as 0.30. Multiply your monthly pay by 0.30.

steps.title: The 40x rule
steps.body:
Many landlords use the **40x rule**: your yearly income before taxes should be at least **40 times the monthly rent**.

Example: rent is $1,000 a month. 40 x $1,000 = $40,000 a year.

If you earn less, many landlords will still rent to you if you have a **co-signer** (also called a **guarantor**): someone with more income who signs too and promises to pay if you don't.
steps.tip: Before you apply, multiply the rent by 40 and compare it with your yearly pay. If you're short, line up a co-signer before you pay any application fee.

steps.prompt: You love an apartment, but your income is below the landlord's 40x rule. What is the usual honest way to still get approved?
options: Ask a parent or other trusted adult to be your co-signer
Round your income up on the application
Offer cash each month with no written lease
Move in first and fill out the application later
feedback: Right. A co-signer with enough income lowers the landlord's risk.
Lying on an application can get you denied, or evicted later if it comes out.
No lease means no protection for you, and most landlords won't agree to it.
Landlords approve tenants before handing over keys.
steps.hint: Think about who could take on the risk if you couldn't pay.
steps.explain: A co-signer is the standard fix. Some landlords also accept a larger deposit instead. Remember that a co-signer's credit is on the line too, so never miss rent.

steps.title: What landlords check
steps.body:
Expect to fill out an application and pay an application fee. Landlords commonly check:
- **Income**: pay stubs or an offer letter
- **Credit report**: late payments and debt
- **Rental history**: references from past landlords
- **Background check**

With no credit or rental history, a **co-signer** (often a parent) agrees to pay if you don't. That is a serious promise for them: missed rent can hurt their credit too.

> Never send a deposit for a place you haven't seen in person or through a trusted contact. Rental listing scams are common.
steps.tip: Check your free credit reports at AnnualCreditReport.com before you apply for apartments, so you can fix any mistakes before a landlord sees them.

steps.title: Read the lease before you sign
steps.body:
A **lease** is a legal contract. Look for:
- **Term**: 12 months is typical. What happens at the end: renews automatically or goes month-to-month?
- **Rent, due date and late fees**
- **Breaking the lease**: what you owe if you move out early
- **Who fixes what**, and how to request repairs
- **Rules**: guests, pets, smoking, subletting
- **Move-out**: notice period and cleaning requirements

Ask questions and get any promises (like "we'll paint before you move in") **in writing**.
steps.tip: Before signing a lease, ask: "What happens if I need to move out early?" Write down the answer, and ask for it in writing if it isn't in the lease.

steps.prompt: Match each rental term to its meaning.
pairs: How long the rental contract lasts
Person who promises to pay if the tenant doesn't
Money held to cover damage or unpaid rent
Renting your place to someone else while you're on the lease
How far ahead you must say you're moving out
steps.explain: Each of these appears in nearly every lease. Knowing the words makes the fine print readable.

steps.prompt: You find a great apartment online for well below market rent. The 'owner' says he is overseas, can't show it, and will mail the keys once you wire the first month's rent and deposit. What do you do?

options.text: Walk away. Can't-show-it plus wire payment plus a too-good price is a classic rental scam.
options.feedback: Right. A real landlord or agent can show the unit or have someone show it, and will accept traceable payment.

options.text: Wire half now and half when the keys arrive.
options.feedback: Wired money is almost impossible to get back. Half is still a loss.

options.text: Ask for a copy of his ID first, then wire the money.
options.feedback: Scammers send fake IDs easily. Seeing the place and confirming ownership matter more.

steps.explain: Rental scams often copy real listings. See it in person, confirm who owns it, and never pay by wire, gift card or crypto.
steps.hint: Count the red flags: you can't see the place, he wants a wire transfer, and the price is far below similar places.

steps.prompt: Which of these should you check in a lease before signing? Select all that apply.
options: The penalty for breaking the lease early
Whether it renews automatically
The landlord's favorite sports team
How to submit repair requests
Late fee amount and grace period
steps.explain: Early termination, renewal, repairs and late fees are where tenants most often get surprised.

steps.title: Key takeaways
steps.body:
- Aim for rent at or below about 30% of gross income.
- Many landlords want yearly income of 40x the rent; a co-signer can help if you're short.
- Count utilities, insurance and commute too.
- Read the whole lease, especially renewal, breaking the lease, repairs and fees.
- Get promises in writing, and never wire money for a place you haven't seen.

levels.title: Deposits, Insurance and Tenant Rights
levels.summary: Move-in inspections, renter's insurance and getting your deposit back.

steps.title: Protect your deposit on day one
steps.body:
Most landlords collect a **security deposit**, often around one month's rent. They can keep part of it for damage beyond normal wear and tear, or unpaid rent.

On move-in day:
- Walk through every room and **take time-stamped photos and video**: walls, floors, appliances, inside cabinets.
- Write down every scratch, stain and broken thing on the move-in checklist.
- Email a copy to the landlord so there is a dated record.

At move-out, do the same after cleaning.
steps.tip: On move-in day, film a slow video of every room, including inside the oven, fridge and cabinets. Email it to yourself and the landlord so it has a date.

steps.prompt: Put these move-in steps in order.
items: Read and sign the lease and pay the deposit
Get the keys and do a walk-through before moving furniture in
Photograph and video every room, noting existing damage
Email the checklist and photos to the landlord
Set up renter's insurance and utilities in your name
steps.explain: Documenting the empty unit before your stuff is in it is the strongest evidence you can have if there's a deposit dispute later.
steps.hint: Paperwork comes first, but you want proof of the empty unit before your stuff goes in.

steps.prompt: Which is most likely **normal wear and tear** that a landlord generally can't charge your deposit for?
options: A large hole in the wall from moving a couch
Lightly worn carpet in a hallway after two years
A cracked bathroom mirror
Burn marks on the countertop
steps.explain: Normal aging from everyday living, like light carpet wear or faded paint, is wear and tear. Holes, cracks and burns are damage.
steps.hint: Wear and tear comes from normal everyday living, not from accidents or misuse.

steps.title: Renter's insurance
steps.body:
Your landlord's insurance covers the **building**, not your stuff. **Renter's insurance** covers:
- **Personal property**: your belongings if stolen or destroyed by fire, smoke, or many kinds of water damage
- **Liability**: if someone is hurt in your apartment or you accidentally damage someone else's property
- **Loss of use**: hotel and meals if your place becomes unlivable

It is usually inexpensive compared with replacing a laptop, phone, and clothes. Floods and earthquakes typically need separate coverage. Some leases require it.
steps.tip: Get two or three renter's insurance quotes online before move-in. Ask what the deductible is (the amount you pay first on each claim).

steps.prompt: A fire in the unit next door causes smoke damage to your clothes, laptop and mattress. You don't have renter's insurance. Who pays to replace your things?

options.text: Most likely you do, because the landlord's policy covers the building, not tenants' belongings.
options.feedback: Correct. That's exactly the gap renter's insurance fills.

options.text: The landlord's insurance automatically replaces everything.
options.feedback: A landlord's policy generally covers the structure, not what tenants own.

options.text: The city pays because it was a fire.
options.feedback: Cities don't replace personal belongings after house fires.

steps.explain: Renter's insurance is one of the cheapest ways to avoid losing thousands of dollars of belongings at once.

steps.title: Tenant rights: check your state
steps.body:
Rules differ a lot by state and city, but common protections include:
- Your home must be **habitable**: working heat, water, plumbing and electrical, and no serious safety hazards.
- Landlords usually must give **notice** before entering, except emergencies.
- After move-out, the landlord must **return your deposit or itemize deductions** within a deadline set by state law.
- Landlords can't **retaliate** against you for requesting legal repairs.

Search your state attorney general or housing agency site for its tenant guide.

> Put repair requests in writing (email or portal) so there is a record.
steps.tip: Search "[your state] tenant rights guide" and save the official state page on your phone before you sign a lease.

steps.prompt: If your landlord ignores a repair request, it's always legal to stop paying rent until it's fixed.
steps.explain: Rent withholding is only allowed in some places, under strict steps. Doing it wrong can get you evicted. Document requests in writing and check your state's rules or a local tenant help line first.

steps.prompt: Match the problem to the best first move.
pairs: Submit a written repair request right away
Give written notice as the lease requires
Ask in writing for it or an itemized list, citing your state's deadline
Turn off the water, then call the landlord's emergency line
steps.explain: Writing creates a record; emergencies need immediate action first, then a call.

steps.prompt: Look up your state's tenant guide. What is the deadline for returning a security deposit, and how much notice must a landlord give before entering?
steps.placeholder: State: ___. Deposit deadline: ___ days. Entry notice: ___.

levels.title: Home Fixes Everyone Should Know
levels.summary: Water shutoffs, the breaker box, clogs and a starter toolkit.

steps.title: Know where to shut things off
steps.body:
Find these the week you move in, before you need them:
- **Fixture shutoff valves**: small valves under sinks and behind the toilet. Turn clockwise to close.
- **Main water shutoff**: stops water to the whole home. Often where the water line enters, near the water heater, or in a utility closet.
- **Breaker box (electrical panel)**: controls power to each circuit.

> If you smell gas (rotten eggs), don't flip switches or light anything. Leave, then call the gas company or 911 from outside.
steps.tip: This week, find the main water shutoff where you live and tie a bright tag or tape on it, so anyone can find it fast in a flood.

steps.prompt: The toilet is about to overflow after you flushed. What do you do first?

options.text: Reach behind the toilet and turn the shutoff valve clockwise to stop the water.
options.feedback: Yes. That stops more water from entering the bowl. Then you can plunge.

options.text: Flush again to clear it.
options.feedback: Flushing again adds another tankful of water and causes the overflow.

options.text: Pour chemical drain cleaner into the bowl.
options.feedback: That doesn't stop the overflow, and splashing chemicals is dangerous.

steps.explain: Stop the water first, then fix the clog. Lifting the tank lid and pushing the flapper down also stops water in a pinch.
steps.hint: What stops more water from coming in?

steps.title: The breaker box
steps.body:
When too much is plugged into one circuit, a **breaker trips** to prevent overheating, and part of your home loses power.

To reset:
1. Unplug or turn off what was running on that circuit.
2. Open the panel and find the breaker that is in the middle or OFF position.
3. Push it **fully to OFF**, then back to **ON**.

If it trips again right away, or you see scorch marks or smell burning, stop and call the landlord or an electrician.

Bathroom and kitchen outlets often have **GFCI** reset buttons on the outlet itself.
steps.tip: Check that every switch in your breaker panel has a label. If not, label them with a friend: one flips a breaker, the other reports which lights and outlets go off.

steps.prompt: The kitchen outlets just lost power while the microwave and toaster were running. Put the fix in order.
items: Unplug the microwave and toaster
Find the tripped breaker in the panel
Push the breaker fully to OFF
Push it back to ON
Plug in one appliance at a time to test
steps.explain: Removing the load first keeps the breaker from tripping again immediately. If it keeps tripping with little plugged in, it's a job for a pro.
steps.hint: Before resetting anything, take away what overloaded the circuit.

steps.title: Clogs: plunger before chemicals
steps.body:
- **Toilet**: use a **flange plunger** (the one with the extra rubber sleeve). Make a seal and push and pull firmly 10-20 times.
- **Sink or tub**: pull out and clean the stopper (hair builds up there), then try a cup plunger or a cheap plastic **drain snake**.
- **Prevention**: no grease down the sink, no wipes or paper towels in the toilet, and a hair catcher in the shower.

Chemical drain cleaners can damage pipes and burn skin. Never mix two different cleaners: some combinations release toxic gas.
steps.tip: Buy a flange plunger and a plastic drain snake before your first clog, not during it. Both are cheap at any hardware store.

steps.prompt: Which belong in a basic starter toolkit for an apartment? Select all that apply.
options: Screwdriver set (flat and Phillips)
Flange plunger
Tape measure
Chainsaw
Adjustable wrench
Flashlight
steps.explain: Screwdrivers, a plunger, tape measure, adjustable wrench, flashlight, plus a hammer, pliers and duct tape cover most small jobs. A chainsaw is not an apartment tool.

steps.prompt: Pouring cooking grease down the sink with hot water is fine because the hot water keeps it liquid.
steps.explain: Grease cools and hardens further down the pipe, building clogs. Let it solidify in a can or jar and throw it in the trash.

steps.prompt: Match each home emergency to the first thing to do.
pairs: Close the shutoff valve or the main water
steps.explain: Knowing the first move ahead of time turns panic into a 30-second fix.

steps.prompt: Walk through your home (or your family's). Where is the main water shutoff, the breaker panel and the toilet shutoff valve? Write their locations.
steps.placeholder: Main water: ___. Breaker panel: ___. Toilet valve: ___.

units.title: Insurance and Healthcare
units.description: Speak the language of health insurance, compare plans, and know where to go when you're sick or hurt.

levels.title: Health Insurance Vocabulary
levels.summary: Premiums, deductibles, copays, coinsurance and the out-of-pocket max.

steps.title: Five words that decide what you pay
steps.body:
- **Premium**: what you pay every month just to have the insurance, even if you never use it.
- **Deductible**: what you pay for covered care each year before the plan starts sharing costs.
- **Copay**: a flat fee for a service, like $30 for a doctor visit.
- **Coinsurance**: your percentage share after the deductible, like 20%.
- **Out-of-pocket maximum**: the most you'll pay for covered in-network care in a year. After that, the plan pays 100%.

Premiums don't count toward the deductible or out-of-pocket max.
steps.tip: Find your health insurance card, then look up your plan's deductible and out-of-pocket max in the insurer's app or website. Save both numbers in your phone notes.

steps.prompt: Match each insurance term to its meaning.
pairs: Monthly cost to keep the plan
Amount you pay before the plan shares costs
Flat fee for a visit or prescription
Your percent of the bill after the deductible
Yearly cap on what you pay for covered care
steps.explain: These five terms are on every plan summary. Once you know them you can compare any two plans.

steps.prompt: Your plan has a $2,000 deductible, and you haven't used any care yet this year. You get a $300 covered urgent care bill (no copay applies). How much do you pay?
options: $300, all of it, because you haven't met your deductible
$0, because you have insurance
$60, your 20% share
$2,000, the whole deductible at once
feedback: Right. Until your covered bills reach $2,000 this year, you pay them yourself.
Insurance doesn't start sharing costs until the deductible is met (except copays and free preventive care).
Coinsurance only starts after the deductible is met.
You pay the deductible bill by bill, not all at once.
steps.hint: The deductible is what you pay first, before the plan starts sharing costs. Have you reached $2,000 yet?
steps.explain: You pay covered bills yourself (at the plan's discounted price) until they add up to the deductible. After that, coinsurance kicks in and you pay only your share, like 20%. Free preventive care, like a yearly checkup, doesn't wait for the deductible.

steps.title: The out-of-pocket maximum protects you
steps.body:
The **out-of-pocket max** is your worst-case cost for covered, in-network care in a year. Deductibles, copays and coinsurance all count toward it.

For 2026 marketplace and most other plans, the legal ceiling is **$10,600 for one person** ($21,200 for a family). Many plans set theirs lower.

> Going **out of network** can cost far more and may not count toward the max. Check that a doctor or hospital is in network before non-emergency care.
steps.tip: Before any non-emergency appointment, search the doctor's or clinic's name on your insurer's website to confirm they are in network.

steps.prompt: Your plan's out-of-pocket max is $6,000. You've already paid $5,400 in deductible and coinsurance this year. Then you get another covered in-network bill where your normal share would be $1,500. How much do you actually pay?
steps.explain:
$6,000 - $5,400 = **$600**. That's all the room left under your cap.

The plan pays the rest of this bill, and 100% of covered in-network care for the rest of the year.
steps.hint: The max is a cap. How much room is left under $6,000 after what you've already paid?

steps.title: Coverage until 26
steps.body:
Under the Affordable Care Act, you can usually stay on a **parent's health plan until you turn 26**, even if you are married, not living at home, or not a student, and even if you could get a plan through your job.

When you age off, you get a **special enrollment period** to pick a new plan through work or HealthCare.gov. Don't let coverage lapse: one ER visit uninsured can cost thousands.
steps.tip: If you're on a parent's plan, put your 26th birthday on your calendar with a reminder two months before, so you can pick your next plan without a gap.

steps.prompt: Your monthly premiums count toward your deductible.
steps.explain: Premiums are the price of having the plan. Only what you pay for care (deductible, copays, coinsurance) counts toward the deductible and out-of-pocket max.

steps.prompt: You see a doctor with a $30 copay listed for office visits. What does the $30 usually mean?
options: You pay $30 for the visit and the plan pays the rest of the visit cost
You pay $30 per month whether you go or not
The visit is free until you've paid $30 in premiums
You pay 30% of the bill
steps.explain: A copay is a flat fee per service. The monthly charge is the premium, and a percentage share is coinsurance. Tests done during the visit may be billed separately.
steps.hint: A copay is a flat fee per visit. What's the monthly charge called?

steps.title: Key takeaways
steps.body:
- Premium = monthly cost; deductible = paid first; coinsurance = your % after that; copay = flat fee.
- The out-of-pocket max caps your yearly cost for covered in-network care.
- Stay in network when you can.
- You can usually stay on a parent's plan until 26.

levels.title: Comparing Health Plans
levels.summary: Low premium vs low deductible, and how to estimate your true yearly cost.

steps.title: There is no free lunch
steps.body:
Plans trade off monthly cost against cost when you use care:
- **Low premium, high deductible**: cheap each month, expensive if you get sick or hurt.
- **High premium, low deductible**: expensive each month, cheaper when you use care.

To compare, estimate your **total yearly cost**:

> Premiums x 12 + what you expect to pay for care

Then check the worst case: premiums x 12 + the out-of-pocket max.
steps.tip: At open enrollment, write each plan's monthly premium, deductible and out-of-pocket max side by side in one note. Comparing three numbers beats reading three brochures.

steps.prompt: Plan A costs $150 a month in premiums. What are its total premiums for the year?
steps.explain:
$150 x 12 = **$1,800** a year, before any care.

Quick check: $100 x 12 = $1,200 and $50 x 12 = $600. Together, $1,800.
steps.hint: There are 12 months in a year. Multiply the monthly premium by 12.

steps.prompt: You want to know a plan's **worst-case** yearly cost, in case you got badly hurt. What do you add up?
options: A full year of premiums + the out-of-pocket max
The deductible only
One month's premium + the deductible
The out-of-pocket max only
feedback: Right. You pay every premium no matter what, and the max caps your care costs.
You could pay more than the deductible: coinsurance continues until the max.
You pay premiums all 12 months, and costs can go past the deductible.
Premiums don't count toward the max, so add them on top.
steps.hint: Worst case means you pay every premium AND hit the yearly cap on care.
steps.explain: Example: $150 a month is $1,800 a year. Add a $6,000 out-of-pocket max: $7,800 worst case for covered in-network care. Make sure your savings could handle that number.

steps.prompt: You're healthy, rarely see a doctor, and have $3,000 in savings. Plan A: $150/month, $3,000 deductible. Plan B: $320/month, $500 deductible. Which is the better fit?

options.text: Plan A. You save $2,040 a year in premiums, and your savings could cover the deductible if something happened.
options.feedback: Good reasoning. Plan B costs $3,840 in premiums vs $1,800; a healthy person rarely makes that back.

options.text: Plan B, because a lower deductible is always better.
options.feedback: You'd pay $2,040 more in premiums every year for protection you probably won't use.

options.text: Neither. Skip insurance and save the money.
options.feedback: A single accident or appendicitis can cost tens of thousands of dollars uninsured.

steps.explain: Low-premium, high-deductible plans fit healthy people with savings. If you have ongoing prescriptions or a planned surgery, run the numbers again: the low-deductible plan may win.
steps.hint: Compare the yearly difference in premiums with how much care you actually expect to use.

steps.title: HDHPs and HSAs
steps.body:
A **high-deductible health plan (HDHP)** that meets IRS rules lets you open a **Health Savings Account (HSA)**.

- For 2026 an HDHP must have a deductible of at least **$1,700** for one person.
- You can put in up to **$4,400** (self-only, 2026).
- Money goes in tax-free, grows tax-free, and comes out tax-free for medical costs. It never expires and stays yours if you change jobs.

An HSA can make a high-deductible plan much more attractive, especially if your employer adds money.
steps.tip: If your employer puts money into an HSA when you pick the high-deductible plan, check that offer before you choose. That deposit is free money for medical costs.

steps.prompt: Which should you check when comparing two health plans? Select all that apply.
options: Whether your current doctors are in network
Monthly premium x 12
Deductible and out-of-pocket max
Whether your prescriptions are covered (the formulary)
The color of the insurance card
steps.explain: Network, total premiums, deductible, out-of-pocket max and drug coverage decide your real cost. The card design doesn't.

steps.prompt: Put these plan-choosing steps in order.
items: List the care you expect next year (visits, prescriptions, procedures)
Check that your doctors and medicines are covered in each plan
Add up yearly premiums for each plan
Estimate expected costs and the worst case (premiums + out-of-pocket max)
Pick the plan with the best mix of expected cost and a worst case you can afford
steps.explain: Start with your needs, filter by coverage, then compare dollars. Repeat every open enrollment, because plans change yearly.
steps.hint: Start with the care you need, then check coverage, then compare dollars.

steps.title: Key takeaways
steps.body:
- Compare total yearly cost, not just the premium.
- Worst case = premiums + out-of-pocket max.
- Healthy with savings? A high-deductible plan with an HSA often wins.
- Regular prescriptions or planned care? Run the numbers on a low-deductible plan.
- Check networks and drug lists every year.

levels.title: Getting the Right Care
levels.summary: Primary care, urgent care vs the ER, and handling appointments and bills.

steps.title: Where to go for care
steps.body:
- **Primary care doctor (PCP)**: checkups, ongoing issues, referrals. Your home base.
- **Telehealth**: video visits for simple problems like rashes, colds or prescription refills.
- **Urgent care**: same-day help for problems that can't wait but aren't life-threatening: sprains, minor cuts that need stitches, flu, ear infections, UTIs.
- **Emergency room (ER)**: life-threatening or severe problems. Much more expensive.

> If it might be life-threatening, call **911** or go to the ER. Never skip the ER to save money in a true emergency.
steps.tip: Save the address and hours of the nearest in-network urgent care in your phone now, so you aren't searching while you're hurt.

steps.prompt: Match each problem to the best place for care.
pairs: Chest pain and shortness of breath
Twisted ankle, can still walk on it
Mild rash you want looked at
steps.explain: Chest pain could be a heart attack: always emergency. Sprains fit urgent care. Routine and minor issues fit your PCP or telehealth.

steps.prompt: Which are signs you should call 911 or go to the ER? Select all that apply.
options: Face drooping, arm weakness or slurred speech
Bleeding that won't stop with firm pressure
A sore throat for two days
Trouble breathing
Confusion after hitting your head
steps.explain: Stroke signs, uncontrolled bleeding, trouble breathing and confusion after a head injury are emergencies. A two-day sore throat can go to urgent care or your PCP.

steps.title: Booking and preparing for an appointment
steps.body:
When you call or book online, have ready:
- Your **insurance card** and photo ID
- The reason for the visit in one sentence
- Your availability

Before the visit, write down:
- Symptoms: when they started, what makes them better or worse
- Medicines and supplements you take, and allergies
- Your questions, most important first

Ask the office if they are **in network** with your plan before you go.
steps.tip: Before your next appointment, type a three-line note in your phone: main symptom, when it started, and your top question. Read it to the doctor.

steps.title: Check the bill before you pay
steps.body:
After a visit, your insurer sends an **Explanation of Benefits (EOB)**. It is not a bill. It shows what was charged, what insurance paid, and what you should owe.

Then the clinic or hospital sends the actual **bill**. Compare the two. Mistakes are common: charges listed twice, or services you never got.

If a correct bill is more than you can pay, ask for a **payment plan** or **financial assistance**. Nonprofit hospitals must offer assistance programs.
steps.tip: Never pay a medical bill until it matches the Explanation of Benefits from your insurer. If the numbers differ, call the billing office and ask for an itemized bill.

steps.prompt: Put these steps for handling a new medical bill in order.
items: Wait for the Explanation of Benefits (EOB) from your insurer
Compare the bill from the provider with the EOB
Call the provider's billing office about any mismatch or error
Ask about a payment plan or financial assistance if you can't pay
Pay the correct amount and keep the records
steps.explain: The EOB shows what insurance paid and what you owe. Billing errors are common, and many hospitals have financial assistance programs if you ask.
steps.hint: The EOB arrives first and tells you what you should owe.

steps.prompt: It's Saturday night. You cut your hand while cooking; it's deep and gaping but stops bleeding with pressure. Your doctor's office is closed. Where do you go?

options.text: An urgent care that's open now, since it probably needs stitches soon but isn't life-threatening.
options.feedback: Good choice. Cuts that gape usually need stitches within hours, and urgent care handles that for much less than the ER.

options.text: Wait until Monday for your regular doctor.
options.feedback: Stitches work best within hours, and waiting raises the risk of infection.

options.text: Super glue it at home and skip care.
options.feedback: A deep, gaping cut needs proper cleaning and closing by a professional.

steps.explain: If the bleeding wouldn't stop with firm pressure, or you couldn't move your fingers normally, that would be ER territory.
steps.hint: Ask two questions: is it life-threatening, and does it need care today?

steps.prompt: In a true emergency, federal law requires ERs to screen and stabilize you even if you can't pay.
steps.explain: The EMTALA law requires hospitals with ERs to provide a medical screening and stabilizing treatment regardless of ability to pay. You may still get a bill, but you can ask about financial assistance.

steps.prompt: Find the nearest urgent care that takes your insurance and its hours. Do you have a primary care doctor? If not, write down one in-network doctor you could book.

units.title: Cars
units.description: Buy a used car without getting burned, keep it running, and know what to do after a crash.

levels.title: Buying a Used Car
levels.summary: Total cost of ownership, inspections, history reports and financing.

steps.title: The price tag is just the start
steps.body:
The **total cost of ownership** is everything a car costs you, not just the price:
- Price, plus sales tax, title and registration
- **Insurance**: can differ by hundreds of dollars a year between cars
- **Gas**: a car that gets 35 miles per gallon (mpg) uses far less than one that gets 20
- **Maintenance and repairs**: oil, tires, brakes, surprises
- **Loan interest** if you borrow

> A cheap car that's pricey to insure or always in the shop can cost more than a reliable one.
steps.tip: Before you test-drive a car, get an insurance quote on it using its year, make and model. It takes about ten minutes and can rule a car out fast.

steps.prompt: Two used cars cost the same. Car A gets 20 mpg. Car B gets 35 mpg. You drive a lot for work. Which costs less to run?
options: Car B, because it uses less gas for every mile
Car A, because a lower mpg number means it burns less fuel
They cost the same to run, since the prices are the same
You can't tell without knowing the colors and trims
feedback: Right. More miles per gallon means fewer gallons to buy.
It's the opposite: mpg is how far you go on one gallon, so higher is better.
Same price to buy doesn't mean same cost to run.
Color and trim don't change fuel use.
steps.hint: mpg means miles per gallon: how far the car goes on one gallon.
steps.explain: Higher mpg means fewer gallons for the same driving. Over 12,000 miles a year, the 20-mpg car burns 600 gallons and the 35-mpg car about 343. At $3 a gallon, that's roughly $770 a year saved.

steps.title: Check it before you buy it
steps.body:
Before you hand over money:
- **Vehicle history report**: run the VIN for accidents, flood or salvage titles and odometer problems.
- **Open recalls**: check the VIN at NHTSA's recall lookup.
- **Test drive**: city and highway, braking, strange noises, warning lights.
- **Pre-purchase inspection** by an independent mechanic you choose (often about $100-200). It's the best money you'll spend.

Walk away if a seller won't allow an inspection.
steps.tip: Before buying a used car, enter its VIN (the 17-character code on the dashboard by the windshield) at nhtsa.gov/recalls to check for unfixed recalls. It's free.

steps.prompt: Put these used-car buying steps in a smart order.
items: Set a total budget, including insurance and repairs
Get pre-approved for a loan from a bank or credit union (if financing)
Shortlist reliable models and get insurance quotes
Check the history report and test drive
Get an independent pre-purchase inspection
Negotiate the out-the-door price and sign
steps.explain: Budget and financing first keep you from being sold a monthly payment. The inspection comes before you negotiate so problems become bargaining points or a reason to walk.
steps.hint: Money decisions come before you fall in love with a car. The inspection comes before you sign.

steps.prompt: At a dealership, the salesperson asks, 'What monthly payment are you looking for?' What's your best answer?

options.text: Say you're focused on the total out-the-door price and already have financing lined up.
options.feedback: Right. Negotiating the payment lets them stretch the loan term or add extras while the payment looks fine.

options.text: Give a monthly number, like $300.
options.feedback: They can hit $300 with a 72- or 84-month loan and a higher price. You pay much more in total.

options.text: Tell them your credit score and income so they can find the best deal.
options.feedback: That helps them structure the deal for themselves. Get your own pre-approval first.

steps.explain: Negotiate one number: the out-the-door price including all fees. Compare dealer financing to your pre-approval.
steps.hint: A monthly payment can be lowered by stretching the loan. Which number can't be stretched?

steps.prompt: The car with the lower price tag is always the cheaper car to own.
steps.hint: Think about the costs that keep coming every year after you buy.
steps.explain: Example: Car A costs $9,000 and $1,200 a year to insure. Car B costs $8,000 but $2,000 a year to insure. After 3 years, Car B has cost $1,400 more. Compare price, insurance, gas and likely repairs together.

steps.prompt: A clean title and a shiny exterior mean a used car has never been in a flood or serious accident.
steps.explain: Not all damage gets reported, and titles can be 'washed' through other states. Use a history report and an independent mechanic's inspection.

steps.title: Key takeaways
steps.body:
- Budget the total cost: price, insurance, fuel, maintenance and interest.
- Get insurance quotes and loan pre-approval before shopping.
- Run the VIN, check recalls, test drive, and get an independent inspection.
- Negotiate the out-the-door price, not the monthly payment.

levels.title: Basic Car Care
levels.summary: Oil, tires, warning lights and how to jump-start a dead battery.

steps.title: The owner's manual is the rulebook
steps.body:
Your car's **owner's manual** lists its maintenance schedule: oil changes, filters, fluids, belts. Many modern cars go 5,000-10,000 miles between oil changes, while older cars may need it sooner. The old "every 3,000 miles" rule is often more than needed.

Monthly habits:
- Check **tire pressure**, including the spare
- Glance at the **oil level** on the dipstick
- Check lights and wipers

A warning light on the dashboard is the car asking for help. A **flashing** check-engine light means pull over safely and get it checked soon.
steps.tip: Set a monthly phone reminder to check your tire pressure (spare too) and glance at the oil dipstick. It takes five minutes at a gas station.

steps.title: Tires: pressure and tread
steps.body:
- Use the pressure on the sticker inside the **driver's door jamb**, not the max number on the tire's sidewall.
- Check when tires are **cold** (before driving), at least monthly.
- Low pressure wears tires faster, hurts mpg, and makes handling worse.

**Tread depth**: 2/32 of an inch is the legal minimum in most states. The **penny test**: put a penny in the tread, Lincoln's head down. If you can see all of his head, the tread is too worn. Many experts suggest replacing sooner for wet roads.
steps.tip: Keep a cheap tire pressure gauge in your glove box. Gas station air pump gauges can be inaccurate.

steps.prompt: Where do you find the correct tire pressure for your car?
options: The maximum PSI printed on the tire sidewall
The sticker in the driver's door jamb or the owner's manual
Whatever the gas station air pump says
Always 40 PSI for any car
steps.explain: The door-jamb sticker shows the carmaker's recommended pressure. The sidewall number is the maximum the tire can safely hold, not the target.
steps.hint: The number on the tire itself is a maximum, not a target.

steps.title: Jump-starting a dead battery
steps.body:
You need jumper cables and a running car (or a portable jump starter). Both cars off, parking brakes on.

Connect in this order:
1. **Red** clamp to the dead battery's **+**
2. Other **red** clamp to the good battery's **+**
3. **Black** clamp to the good battery's **-**
4. Last **black** clamp to bare, unpainted metal on the dead car, away from the battery

Start the good car, wait a few minutes, then try the dead one. Remove clamps in **reverse** order. Check your manual first: some cars have special jump points.
steps.tip: Put jumper cables or a charged portable jump starter in your trunk this week. A dead battery is easy to fix when you already have them.

steps.prompt: Put the jumper cable connections in the correct order.
items: Red clamp on the dead battery's positive (+) terminal
Other red clamp on the good battery's positive (+) terminal
Black clamp on the good battery's negative (-) terminal
Last black clamp on bare metal on the dead car, away from the battery
Start the working car and let it run a few minutes
steps.explain: Connecting the last clamp to bare metal away from the battery keeps any spark away from battery gases.
steps.hint: Red (positive) goes on first. The very last clamp goes somewhere away from the battery.

steps.prompt: Your owner's manual says to change the oil every 7,500 miles. A quick-lube shop puts a sticker on your windshield saying come back in 3,000 miles. What should you follow?
options: The owner's manual or the car's oil-life reminder
The shop sticker, since the shop knows best
Change it every 1,000 miles to be extra safe
Wait until a red oil light comes on
feedback: Right. The carmaker built that schedule for your exact engine.
Shops often default to short intervals. Your manual is the rulebook.
That wastes money and oil without helping the engine.
A red oil light can mean low oil pressure. Stop soon and check it; don't use it as a schedule.
steps.hint: Who wrote the maintenance schedule for your exact car?
steps.explain: Follow the manual or the oil-life reminder. If you mostly drive in hard conditions (towing, dusty roads, lots of very short trips), the manual may list a shorter interval for that.

steps.prompt: While driving on the highway, your check-engine light starts **flashing** and the car feels like it's shaking. What do you do?

options.text: Slow down, pull over safely, and get the car checked before driving it much further.
options.feedback: Right. A flashing light usually means a serious misfire that can damage the engine and catalytic converter.

options.text: Keep driving normally and book a check-up next month.
options.feedback: A flashing light is more urgent than a steady one. Driving on can turn a small repair into a big one.

options.text: Turn the radio up so you don't hear it.
options.feedback: Ignoring the warning risks expensive damage and a breakdown in traffic.

steps.explain: Steady check-engine light: get it checked soon. Flashing: pull over safely and address it now. Red oil or temperature lights also mean stop soon.
steps.hint: Flashing is more urgent than steady.

steps.prompt: You should check tire pressure right after a long highway drive for the most accurate reading.
steps.explain: Driving heats tires and raises pressure. Check cold, before driving or after the car has sat a few hours.

steps.prompt: Find your car's (or a family car's) recommended tire pressure on the door sticker and its oil change interval in the manual. Write them down.
steps.placeholder: Front PSI: ___ Rear PSI: ___ Oil change every ___ miles.

levels.title: Car Insurance and Accidents
levels.summary: Coverage types, deductibles, and the steps to take after a crash.

steps.title: Car insurance coverages
steps.body:
Almost every state requires **liability** insurance. Main types:
- **Liability**: pays for injuries and damage you cause to others. Required; state minimums are often too low to cover a serious crash.
- **Collision**: repairs your car after a crash, no matter who's at fault.
- **Comprehensive**: theft, hail, fire, vandalism, hitting a deer.
- **Uninsured/underinsured motorist**: covers you when the other driver has no or too little insurance.

Collision and comprehensive have a **deductible**: you pay that much per claim first. Lenders require them if you finance.
steps.tip: Open your car insurance app or card and check your liability limits. If they're only the state minimum, ask your agent what higher limits would cost.

steps.prompt: Match each event to the coverage that pays.
pairs: You rear-end someone and damage their car
Hail dents your car in a parking lot
You slide into a pole and dent your own car
A driver with no insurance hits you
steps.explain: Liability covers others; collision covers your car in crashes; comprehensive covers non-crash damage.
steps.hint: Liability is for damage you cause to others. Comprehensive is for damage that isn't a crash.

steps.prompt: You have a $500 collision deductible. You back into a pole and the repair costs $1,800. How much does insurance pay?
steps.explain:
You pay the first $500.

Insurance pays $1,800 - $500 = **$1,300**.

A higher deductible lowers your premium but means more out of pocket for each claim.
steps.hint: You pay the deductible first. Insurance pays the rest of the repair.

steps.title: After a crash: stay calm, stay safe
steps.body:
1. **Check for injuries**. Call 911 if anyone is hurt.
2. **Get safe**: if the cars can move and it's minor, move out of traffic. Hazard lights on.
3. **Call police** if required in your state or if there are injuries or major damage. Get the report number.
4. **Exchange info**: names, phone, insurance company and policy number, license plate.
5. **Document**: photos of both cars, plates, the scene, damage; get witness contacts.
6. **Report** to your insurer promptly.

Stick to facts. Don't argue about who was at fault at the scene.
steps.tip: Save a crash checklist in your phone notes now: injuries, safety, police report number, other driver's info, photos, call insurer. You won't think clearly right after a crash.

steps.prompt: Put these after-crash steps in order.
items: Check yourself and others for injuries and call 911 if anyone is hurt
Move to a safe spot if possible and turn on hazard lights
Exchange names, insurance and plate numbers with the other driver
Take photos of the cars, plates and scene
Call your insurance company to report the claim
steps.explain: People first, safety second, information and evidence third, then the insurer.

steps.prompt: After a minor fender-bender, the other driver says, 'Let's not involve insurance. I'll just pay you cash for the damage.' What's the smartest move?

options.text: Still exchange full insurance info, take photos, and get a written repair estimate before agreeing to anything.
options.feedback: Smart. Hidden damage and injuries can show up later, and you need info to file a claim if the cash never comes.

options.text: Agree, shake hands, and leave without their information.
options.feedback: If they never pay or later claim you caused it, you have nothing to go on.

options.text: Apologize and say it was all your fault so things stay friendly.
options.feedback: Let the facts and insurers decide fault. Be polite, but stick to what happened.

steps.explain: You can still settle privately, but always collect information and evidence first. Some states also require you to report crashes above a damage amount.
steps.hint: What would you need if the cash never comes, or an injury shows up later?

steps.prompt: Your state's minimum liability coverage is always enough to cover a serious accident.
steps.explain: Minimums can be far below the cost of a serious crash. If you cause more damage than your limits, you can be personally responsible for the rest. Many people choose higher limits.

steps.title: Key takeaways
steps.body:
- Liability covers others; collision and comprehensive cover your car.
- Your deductible comes out first on each claim.
- After a crash: injuries, safety, info, photos, insurer.
- Keep your insurance card and registration in the car, and a crash checklist in your phone.

units.title: Kitchen and Paperwork
units.description: Eat well for less, keep food safe, and keep your important documents and contracts under control.

levels.title: Groceries and Meal Planning on a Budget
levels.summary: Plan meals, compare unit prices and cook a few flexible base recipes.

steps.title: Plan first, shop second
steps.body:
Eating out a few times a week adds up fast. A weekly plan saves money and time:
1. Check what you already have.
2. Pick 3-4 dinners that share ingredients (one bag of spinach, three meals).
3. Plan leftovers for lunches.
4. Write a list and stick to it.

Budget staples: rice, oats, pasta, dried or canned beans, lentils, eggs, frozen vegetables, bananas, potatoes, peanut butter, chicken thighs, canned tuna.

> Frozen vegetables are picked ripe, last for months and are just as nutritious.
steps.tip: Before your next grocery trip, take a photo of your fridge and pantry so you don't buy what you already have.

steps.title: Compare unit prices
steps.body:
The shelf tag usually shows a **unit price**: cost per ounce, pound or count. It lets you compare different sizes and brands fairly.

> Unit price = price / quantity

Bigger is often cheaper per unit, but not always, and it's only a deal if you use it before it goes bad. Store brands are often much cheaper than name brands for nearly the same product.
steps.tip: Next time you shop, read the small unit-price number on the shelf tag (like 18¢/oz) instead of the big price. Compare two sizes of something you buy often.

steps.prompt: The shelf tags say: 24 oz peanut butter, $4.80 (20¢ per oz). 32 oz peanut butter, $5.76 (18¢ per oz). You eat a lot of peanut butter. Which is the better deal?
options: The 32 oz jar, because it costs less per ounce
The 24 oz jar, because its price is lower
They're the same deal
You can't tell without doing long division
feedback: Right. 18¢ an ounce beats 20¢ an ounce.
A lower price for less food isn't a better deal. Compare per ounce.
The unit prices are different: 18¢ vs 20¢.
The store already did the math. The unit price is on the tag.
steps.hint: Ignore the big price. Which jar costs less for each ounce you get?
steps.explain: The unit price lets you compare different sizes fairly. The bigger jar only wins if you'll use it before it goes bad, which is easy with peanut butter but harder with fresh food.

steps.prompt: You spend $14 on takeout lunch 4 days a week. Packing lunch costs about $4. How much do you save per week by packing?
steps.explain:
Each day: $14 - $4 = $10 saved.

4 days x $10 = **$40 a week**. Over a year, that's roughly $2,000.
steps.hint: First find how much you save on one day. Then multiply by the number of days.

steps.title: Three base recipes that adapt
steps.body:
Learn a few patterns, not just recipes:
- **Sheet-pan dinner**: chopped vegetables and a protein tossed in oil, salt and spices; roast at about 425°F until browned and cooked through.
- **Stir-fry or rice bowl**: cook protein, add vegetables, add a sauce (soy sauce, garlic, a little sugar or honey), serve over rice.
- **Pot of beans or lentil soup**: onion, garlic, canned tomatoes, beans or lentils, broth, spices. Simmer. Makes many meals.

Swap whatever is on sale into the pattern.
steps.tip: Pick one base recipe this week, like a sheet-pan dinner, and cook a double batch. Pack the extra into containers for two lunches.

steps.prompt: Which are good ways to cut grocery costs? Select all that apply.
options: Plan meals that share ingredients
Shop hungry without a list
Compare unit prices and try store brands
Buy frozen vegetables and fruit
Buy a giant bag of fresh produce you won't finish
steps.explain: Planning, unit prices, store brands and frozen produce save money. Shopping hungry and buying food that spoils waste it.

steps.prompt: Put a weekly meal-planning routine in order.
items: Check the fridge, freezer and pantry
Pick meals that use what you have and share ingredients
Write a grocery list by store section
Shop with the list
Prep ingredients or cook a batch for the week
steps.explain: Starting with what you own avoids buying duplicates and throwing food away.

steps.prompt: It's Thursday, you're tired, and your plan says stir-fry. Your phone shows a $22 delivery order is two taps away. What's the best move?

options.text: Make a fast fallback meal you keep stocked, like eggs and toast or a frozen-veg rice bowl, and save the delivery for a planned treat.
options.feedback: That's the trick: have a 10-minute backup meal for low-energy nights.

options.text: Order delivery and throw out the stir-fry ingredients.
options.feedback: You pay twice: once for the groceries that spoil and once for delivery.

options.text: Skip dinner.
options.feedback: Skipping meals often leads to bigger, pricier snacking later.

steps.explain: Plans fail on tired nights, so plan for those nights too. Budgeting a few treat meals a month keeps it sustainable.
steps.hint: Which choice still feeds you tonight without wasting the groceries you already bought?

steps.prompt: Plan three dinners for next week that share at least two ingredients. Write the meals and the shopping list.

levels.title: Food Safety
levels.summary: Safe cooking temperatures, the 2-hour rule and avoiding cross-contamination.

steps.title: Clean, separate, cook, chill
steps.body:
Food poisoning mostly comes from four mistakes. The USDA fixes:
- **Clean**: wash hands for 20 seconds, and wash cutting boards and counters.
- **Separate**: keep raw meat away from ready-to-eat food. Use a different cutting board, or wash between uses.
- **Cook**: to a safe internal temperature, checked with a **food thermometer**. Color is not a reliable test.
- **Chill**: fridge at **40°F or below**, freezer at 0°F.

Bacteria grow fastest between 40°F and 140°F, the **danger zone**.
steps.tip: Put a cheap fridge thermometer in your fridge and check that it reads 40°F or below. Turn the dial colder if it doesn't.

steps.title: Safe internal temperatures
steps.body:
Measure in the thickest part, away from bone:
- **Poultry** (chicken, turkey, including ground): **165°F**
- **Ground beef and pork**: **160°F**
- **Whole cuts** of beef, pork, lamb (steaks, chops, roasts): **145°F**, then rest **3 minutes**
- **Fish**: **145°F**
- **Leftovers and casseroles**: reheat to **165°F**

A basic instant-read thermometer is cheap and removes the guessing.
steps.tip: Buy an instant-read food thermometer and use it the next time you cook chicken or burgers. Push it into the thickest part.

steps.prompt: Match each food to its USDA minimum safe internal temperature.
steps.explain: Ground meat needs a higher temperature than whole cuts because grinding mixes surface bacteria all the way through.

steps.title: The 2-hour rule
steps.body:
Perishable food (meat, dairy, cooked rice and pasta, cut fruit, leftovers) should not sit out at room temperature for more than **2 hours**, or **1 hour** if it's above 90°F, like at a summer picnic or in a hot car.

After that, throw it out. Reheating doesn't always make it safe, because some bacteria make toxins that heat doesn't destroy.

Refrigerate leftovers in shallow containers so they cool quickly, and eat them within **3-4 days**.

> When in doubt, throw it out.

source.label: USDA FSIS: Leftovers and food safety

steps.tip: After a meal or party, set a phone timer for 2 hours (1 hour on days above 90°F) to remind you to put leftovers in the fridge.

steps.prompt: You get home from a party at 1 a.m. The leftover pizza and chicken wings have been on the counter since 8 p.m. What do you do?

options.text: Throw them out: they've been in the danger zone for about 5 hours.
options.feedback: Right. Far past 2 hours, and smelling fine doesn't mean safe.

options.text: Refrigerate them now; the fridge will kill the bacteria.
options.feedback: Cold slows bacteria but doesn't kill them or undo toxins that already formed.

options.text: Reheat them in the microwave tomorrow until they're hot.
options.feedback: Some bacterial toxins survive reheating.

steps.explain: The 2-hour clock is about time in the danger zone, not how the food looks or smells.
steps.hint: Count the hours the food sat in the danger zone.

steps.prompt: You set out potato salad at a backyard party at 2:00 p.m. It's 95°F outside. By what time should it go back in the cooler or fridge?
options: 3:00 p.m. (1 hour)
4:00 p.m. (2 hours)
6:00 p.m. (4 hours)
Whenever it starts to smell off
feedback: Right. Above 90°F the limit is 1 hour.
2 hours is the limit at normal room temperature, not on a 95°F day.
That's far too long in the danger zone.
Bacteria that cause food poisoning usually don't change the smell.
steps.hint: Above 90°F, the usual 2-hour limit gets shorter.
steps.explain: USDA's rule: perishable food can sit out 2 hours, or only **1 hour** above 90°F. Keep cold food in a cooler on ice and bring out small amounts at a time.

steps.prompt: If chicken is no longer pink inside, it's definitely safe to eat.
steps.explain: Color isn't reliable: chicken can look done before reaching 165°F, or stay pinkish after. A food thermometer is the only reliable test.

steps.prompt: You're making chicken stir-fry. Put the safe-handling steps in order.
items: Wash your hands
Cut the vegetables on a clean board first
Cut the raw chicken last on that board, or use a separate board
Wash the board, knife and your hands with hot soapy water
Cook the chicken until a thermometer reads 165°F
steps.explain: Cutting vegetables before raw meat avoids carrying raw-meat juices onto food that won't be cooked as hot.
steps.hint: Food that won't be cooked hot should touch the board before raw meat does.

steps.title: Key takeaways
steps.body:
- Clean, separate, cook, chill.
- Poultry 165°F, ground meat 160°F, whole cuts and fish 145°F, leftovers 165°F.
- 2 hours out max, 1 hour above 90°F.
- Leftovers: 3-4 days in the fridge.
- Use a thermometer, not color.

levels.title: Documents, Contracts and Fine Print
levels.summary: Keep key documents safe, get a passport, and read before you sign.

steps.title: Documents you'll need again and again
steps.body:
Know where these are, and keep originals in one safe, dry place (a fire-resistant folder or box):
- **Birth certificate**
- **Social Security card**: don't carry it in your wallet. Memorize the number and share it only when truly required (employer, bank, taxes).
- **Passport**
- **Driver's license or state ID**
- **Car title** and insurance documents
- **Health insurance card** and vaccination records

Keep secure digital copies too. Shred papers with personal info before throwing them out.
steps.tip: This week, put your birth certificate, Social Security card and passport into one folder in a safe spot at home, and tell a parent where it is.

steps.prompt: Which should you usually **not** carry in your wallet every day? Select all that apply.
options: Social Security card
Birth certificate
Driver's license
Health insurance card
Passport (when you're not traveling)
steps.explain: Your SSN card, birth certificate and passport are hard to replace and valuable to identity thieves. Your license and insurance card are meant to be carried.

steps.title: Getting your first adult passport
steps.body:
A first adult passport book must be applied for **in person** at an acceptance facility (often a post office or library) using **Form DS-11**. Bring proof of citizenship (like your birth certificate), photo ID, a passport photo, and two separate payments.

Current fees for a first adult passport book: **$130** to the State Department plus a **$35** acceptance fee. Adult passports last 10 years. Apply months before any trip: processing takes weeks.
steps.tip: If you might travel abroad in the next year, start your passport now. Book an appointment at a post office or library that accepts passport applications.

steps.prompt: You're 18 and have never had a passport. How do you apply?
options: In person at an acceptance facility, using Form DS-11
Online, by uploading a selfie
By mailing in a renewal form
At the airport on the day of your trip
feedback: Right. First-time adult applicants apply in person.
Online renewal is only for people who already have an adult passport.
Renewal forms are for people who already have a passport.
Airports don't issue regular passports, and processing takes weeks.
steps.hint: First-time adult applicants must prove citizenship and identity face to face.
steps.explain: Bring Form DS-11, proof of citizenship (like your birth certificate), photo ID, a passport photo and two payments: $130 to the State Department and $35 to the facility, $165 total.

steps.title: Read before you sign
steps.body:
Phone plans, gym memberships, car loans, leases and apps all come with contracts. Before you sign or click agree, look for:
- **Total cost**, not just the monthly price, and when promo pricing ends
- **Length** and **automatic renewal**
- **Cancellation**: how, how much notice, any fee
- **Fees**: late, early termination, activation
- **Arbitration** clauses that limit suing

If a salesperson promises something, get it in the written contract. Take a photo or keep a copy of everything you sign.
steps.tip: Before you start any free trial, set a phone reminder for two days before it ends, so you can cancel if you don't want to pay.

steps.prompt: A gym offers $10/month. The contract says 24-month term, $49 annual fee, auto-renews, and cancellation requires a certified letter 30 days in advance. What should you do?

options.text: Calculate the real cost (24 x $10 + 2 x $49 = $338), decide if you'll really use it that long, and put the cancellation deadline in your calendar if you join.
options.feedback: Exactly. The real price is the total, and auto-renewal deadlines are easy to miss.

options.text: Sign it; $10 a month is too cheap to matter.
options.feedback: The fine print turns $10 into $338 over two years, and you might keep paying after that.

options.text: Sign it and just stop paying if you quit going.
options.feedback: Unpaid contract fees can go to collections and damage your credit.

steps.explain: Find the total cost, the commitment length and the exit before you sign.
steps.hint: Add up every payment over the whole contract, then look at how you get out.

steps.prompt: A phone plan is $35/month for the first 12 months, then $55/month. What will you pay over 24 months?
steps.explain:
First year: 12 x $35 = $420.

Second year: 12 x $55 = $660.

Total: $420 + $660 = **$1,080**. That's an average of $45 a month, not $35.
steps.hint: Split it into two parts: the first 12 months and the next 12 months. Add them.

steps.prompt: It's safe to throw old bank statements and medical bills in the regular trash without shredding them.
steps.explain: Account numbers, addresses and medical details help identity thieves. Shred them, or keep them if you still need the record.

steps.prompt: Do you know where your birth certificate, Social Security card and passport are right now? Write where you'll keep them, and one subscription or contract you'll check for auto-renewal.
steps.placeholder: My documents live in ___. Subscription to check: ___ (renews on ___).
